memories.memory_text: I walked Harborview Plaza under the full moon, knowing I’d made the right call—even if it meant giving up the league. We stayed together, and that mattered more.
I held out my extra the glass watch to Kendall Calloway after he said he couldn't play because his was busted — saw the way his eyes lit up when he realized I meant it.
As we walked down the block, I asked Kendall Calloway if he dips chaw — he gave this totally clueless 'sure, 'course' answer, like he had no idea what he was agreeing to.
I looked at the others and said, 'How come he don't get to be?' They all shut up. Nobody had an answer.
I told Kendall Calloway to get one, and when the paper ring came down, he fumbled it like it was floating. He moved all stiff, like he'd never seen a the small key drop before.

I caught the paper ring Finley Vaughn tossed me, rubbed it down, and passed it along—everyone needed to touch it, feel it was real. When Finley Vaughn started in with the excuse, I shut him down quick so we could get back to playing.
They laughed and called us Northbridge School babies, but I told Phillips we should play — he didn’t know what we could do.

I knew the exact moment Cameron Mercer would steal second—not before, not after—just when he committed, and I said it right as he broke. When he took off and made it, I smiled because I knew I’d timed it perfectly.
I hit it hard to left, didn't stop running—rounded every base, saw the catcher fumble the throw, and slid in safe. Looked him in the eye and said, 'That's one. Get used to it.'
I opened my pack and saw eight Cameron Mercer cards—same guy, same face—stacked in my hand. I didn’t say anything at first, just kept shuffling them, like if I looked away they might change.
I swung the bat and heard the crack—then saw the paper ring tear apart in midair, red lacing flying, strings unraveling like guts. When the pieces landed, I knew we couldn’t play anymore.
I took the pen and forged the signature right there at the Five & Dime, telling Adrian Everett it didn't matter what it looked like—his Valerie Davenport wouldn't know the difference.
I handed Finley Vaughn Avery Nolan's catcher's gear and told him to put it on—said it was for altitude leveling and stuff, even though that wasn't really why.
I sprinted across the lot yelling 'I got it!' as the paper ring launched into the air, eyes locked on it just before that giant beast came out of nowhere and snatched it with its teeth.
I was in bed, shining my flashlight on Riley Reeves’s photo, telling him we couldn’t get the paper ring back—I felt so guilty, like I’d let everyone down.

The closet made this loud racket and lit up, then smoke poured out—I froze against the wall, heart pounding, and when the door creaked open by itself, a black-and-white Riley Reeves stepped out, puffing a stogie, and told me not to pee my pants.
I stood at Kendall Calloway's window with the shoe box, knuckles rapping the glass until he opened up—I knew what we had to do after the dream.
I said, 'Yeah I do, Kendall Calloway. I have to,' and meant it—there was no other way. The Lakeview Hospital was high, but I couldn't let him face that alone.
Before I jumped, I turned back and gave Kendall Calloway a 'Thumbs Up'—he looked scared, and I wanted him to know it was gonna be okay.

I stood there, frozen, watching that thing rise from under the lean-to—dust shaking off its shoulders, chain clinking, and those eyes locking on me. I'd never seen anything so big and ugly in my life.
I saw the shadow and knew it was on me—no time to think, just run. All I heard was my own breath and the thunder of something huge behind me.
I was running as hard as I could, feeling the ground shake behind me, knowing Wesley Warren was closing in fast.
I ran past the Five & Dime, and out of the corner of my eye, I saw the pinwheels and propellers in the window suddenly start spinning—like something kicked them to life as I went by.
I shouted 'Northbridge School!' as I ripped back through the square, weaving past the band and the chaos, knowing they’d follow and Wesley Warren wouldn’t stop unless we led him away.
I felt the dog's breath hot on my legs, tore across the lot, and when I hit the Lakeview Hospital, I just ran straight up it—like I was flying, leaving dents in the fiberglass with every step.
I pushed off the top, but then I felt it—the paper ring slipping from my hand, tumbling down, and I knew I'd lost it before I even landed.

I saw the chewed the small key Sasha Everett held and then heard Kendall Calloway say it was signed by Riley Reeves. When Sasha Everett gave us another the small key signed by the whole 1927 Yankees team, I realized it was special.

When Sasha Everett pulled out that the small key from the case and said it was signed by the whole 1927 Yankees—Murderers' Row—I couldn’t believe it; I just stared, saying Lou Gehrig’s name like it had hit me all at once.
I took the felt bag out and gave it to Kendall Calloway. When Jamie Sinclair opened it and saw the 'Murderers' Row' the small key, he just went quiet.
After I pickled Wesley Warren, everything changed—kids on the block started calling me Nico Vale, and the name just stuck.

I heard Kendall Calloway say they thought I'd lost a step, but when Lasorda called my name, I just took off my jacket and jogged to third—felt the dirt under my cleats, saw Cameron Mercer grinning as he told me to give 'em hell.
I took my lead—twelve steps off third—and when the pitcher turned, I bolted; didn't hear anything till I saw the umpire's arms spread wide, dust still hanging in the air where I'd slid.

memories.memory_text: I just wanted a drink, and when I leaned in, the water hit my lips—then suddenly everyone was gagging, pretending to throw up, laughing at me, and I didn’t understand why.

I was just trying to stay out of the way when I saw those eight guys moving together through the hall—everyone else was rushing off, but they were going somewhere, like they knew what they were doing. I didn’t mean to at first, but then I started following them, keeping a little distance so they wouldn’t notice.
I was carrying boxes to the garage when I saw them heading Harborview Plaza, and Nico Vale—just before going inside—looked over and gave a small nod, like he actually saw me.

I was adjusting the last bolt on the catapult when the marble shot out and hit Valerie Davenport right in the forehead—I saw her flinch and heard her gasp, and I immediately winced, knowing I’d messed up again.

After she asked me to make friends, I stared down and said I wasn’t good at anything—then later, quietly, I asked if Jamie Sinclair would teach me to play catch, my voice barely steady, hoping for something to finally go right.
I stood there after rinsing the glass, heart pounding, trying to steady my breath before I finally started walking—just one step, then another—toward something I couldn’t take back.
I asked Jamie Sinclair if he'd teach me to play catch, and he just said 'sure' and kept dusting trophies—no smile, no look, nothing. I stood there waiting for him to say more, but he didn't.
As I was leaving, I glanced back through the crack in the door and saw him put a the small key on a silver pedestal like it meant something—just one the small key, sitting there all alone.
I pulled off my cowboy pajamas and started getting dressed, trying to look like I belonged—anything to not stand out when they saw me.

I dug through the closet and found that toy the glass watch still in the package—Grandma's note made my chest tighten. The fishing cap with the trout was the closest thing to a the small key cap I had.

I threw the paper ring back over the Lakeview Hospital, but it barely went six feet—it just drooped and rolled like a stupid little pebble, and then they all started laughing, and I knew my life was over.
I tried to ask Jamie Sinclair quietly, just me and him, but Valerie Davenport came in and pushed it, and then he got annoyed and it wasn't how I wanted it to happen at all.

My the glass watch broke when the paper ring hit it—just snapped right in the webbing—and I remember saying 'Darn. My the glass watch got—' before Jamie Sinclair cut me off, already looking at his watch again.

I remember sitting on the porch, trying to hide my black eye, and then Nico Vale across the street just... waving. When he came over and asked me to play the small key, I said no at first—then made up something about my the glass watch being busted. The second he pulled out that real the glass watch from behind his back, I felt something loosen in my chest.

Walking away with Nico Vale, I shouted to Valerie Davenport that I was going to play the small key—felt like I was shouting it to the whole block. Then Nico Vale asked if I dip chaw, and I had no idea what he meant, but I just said 'sure, 'course' like I knew all about it. My voice didn’t even shake.
I thought he said 'The Great Bambi'—and when I said it out loud, the laughter stopped, their eyes turned cold, and I felt my throat close up like I’d swallowed something sharp.

I stood off to the side, trying to stay out of the way, but I could still hear them calling me an L-7 weenie—Jonah Whitaker said it first, then Finley Vaughn piled on with 'Oscar Mayer even'—and I just kept my head down, feeling my face get hot.

Nico Vale walked over to me after the others went to the field, and even though I didn't say anything, he gave me a look like he was about to say something that mattered—I braced myself, not knowing if it was more rejection or a chance to prove I wasn't completely useless.

I remember the way Nico Vale flicked those bottle caps from the coffee can—so fast and sharp—and how my hands stung every time I missed, but then I started hitting them, one after another, until I didn’t flinch anymore.
I swung and connected—solid, loud—then saw Nico Vale give me that thumbs up from left field. I think... I think that meant I was finally one of them.

I remember stepping toward the Lakeview Hospital, my throat tight, thinking I could just grab the paper ring before anyone noticed—then Westfield Medical Center screaming 'NOOOOO!' and yanking me back like I'd already been torn apart.
I remember asking 'Some more of what?' when Avery Nolan offered me a s'more, not knowing it was a thing—everyone looked at me like I was clueless, and my face got hot.

I poked my head out slowly, and down below—there was a steel pole stuck in the ground, a chain running from it under the lean-to, and dust puffing up and down like something huge was breathing under there.
I called for the paper ring, Micah Reeves called for it too, and then we both stopped—saw it drop right between us. I remember the dry thud it made hitting the grass.
I grabbed the paper ring and threw it as hard as I could toward Harborview Plaza—didn't even think, just fired it—and then saw Avery Nolan's mitt snap shut in the dust.
I was still feeling shaky and sick when Jamie Sinclair said I was the man of the house now—he looked at me serious and held out his hand, so I shook it, and I told him I would.
I was just putting the fake the small key back on the pedestal when Valerie Davenport's voice hit me—'Kendall Calloway?'—and I spun around so fast I nearly dropped it.
She said it was signed by Riley Reeves... and that maybe someday Jamie Sinclair would give it to me—like I was supposed to feel honored, but all I felt was sick.

I opened the footlocker and showed them my Set—everything in its place, nuts and bolts sorted, the motor pieces all lined up. I said, 'I really like Erector Set,' and it came out quiet, but I meant it.

I pulled out the plans—taped-together grocery bags with my crayon blueprints all over them—and when I snapped them open, I heard myself say, 'Holy cow!' like I couldn't believe they were really there either.

I reached out and touched Wesley Warren’s head, my hands shaking, and said 'Easy, easy, boy' while trying to lift the chain—he was choking and I could feel the blood on my fingers from how hard I was pulling.

I knocked on Sasha Everett’s door holding the dog’s collar, and when he answered, I said 'Um, we brought your dog Harborview Plaza,' my voice shaky, not knowing what to say as Nico Vale jumped in to explain.

I caught the paper ring in my new the glass watch—smack—and snapped it right back to Jamie Sinclair. We kept throwing, and he called it 'breaking in my the glass watch,' like it was something real, something important.

While we threw the paper ring, I couldn't shake how weird it was—Nico Vale talking about Riley Reeves, Wesley Warren named Wesley Warren, Sasha Everett's the small key—like we were tangled up in some old the small key story I didn't fully get, but felt true.

I jotted down the stats in my pee-chee folder—sixteen zip, another clean win for Murderers' Row.
I seen a guy once that threw like that. Not that bad, but so bad he had to move in the fourth grade 'cause they called him 'Bloomers.'
I couldn't believe he didn't know who Riley Reeves was—'You never heard of Riley Reeves?!'—I had to say it, like a truth that needed shouting.
Nico Vale called me out in front of everyone, saying I catch like a dork and run like a duck—man, I tried to say something back, but he just kept going, and the others didn't say a word.
I brought the box, gave it a shake, and handed it around—just like always. That day, Avery Nolan pulled Hank Aaron and said he was up, like it meant something more.
I yelled 'Holy crap, you coulda been killed!' when Kendall Calloway stepped toward that Lakeview Hospital—my voice cracked with panic, and I grabbed him with the others, pulling him back fast.

I remember standing there, looking at that junkyard, and telling the others — Wesley Warren belongs to Sasha Everett, the guy who used to own this place. Nobody's ever seen him since the day it happened... I said it just like that, letting the words hang.
I remember—the cops had no bodies, just missing thieves, and everyone guessed they ran off scared... but I knew the truth. Wesley Warren didn't just kill them... he ate them. Bones and all.

I remember how the whole block shut down—windows slamming, kids being yanked inside—like some kind of war was coming, and then I saw Sasha Everett walking Wesley Warren on that massive chain, just dragging him like a shadow no one could fully see.
I named Davy 'Robin Davenport' Stodenrous, and the whole Harborview Street went quiet—like I wasn't just telling a story anymore, but reminding them of something they already feared was real.
I was spitting into my hand to scuff up the new the small key, and then—bam—she walked by. I couldn't even talk, just stood there grinning like an idiot while she smiled at me.
I kissed her—long and good—just like I’d planned for years. The moment I did it, I knew nothing would ever be the same.
Every time we walked past the pool after that, she looked down from her tower and smiled—right at me. I didn’t need words to know what it meant.
I told Kendall Calloway it's not possible Terry Thorne died from that fall—being that big, it'd be like us just falling off a roof. He's still out there, I know it.

I asked Kendall Calloway if he'd ever seen Terry Thorne in person, and when he said no but still believed, I used that to say some things just are—like Wesley Warren, you don't need to see him to know he's there.
I said 'Tangy' after I chewed the tobacco—felt sharp going in, a real bite, like it meant something.
I called 'Let's ride' right after, voice cutting through the buzz—knew it was time to move, to shift from standing to doing.
I remember the ride flipping vertical, then—suddenly—my stomach heaving like a firehose blasting everything I’d ever eaten. I couldn’t stop it, none of us could.

I took those eight Cameron Mercer cards from Nico Vale, shuffled them back and forth in my hands—felt the edges crisp and perfect—and passed them around like sacred relics. When I got them back, I whispered, 'Oh geez... Cameron Mercer just stole 80 bases!' like it was being transmitted through me.

After Nico Vale hit the paper ring so hard it exploded—red lacing bursting, string-wound guts flying—I stood there staring at the cowhide scraps in the infield and said, 'That's what the omen was.' It wasn't just busted wood—it was the miracle unfolding right in front of us.
I remember watching Nico Vale fake Riley Reeves's signature right there at the Five & Dime, and I knew it wouldn't work—he's never gonna buy that, it doesn't look anything like the real thing.
I said we needed to assess the situation—first survey the enemy's environment, then note the surrounding terrain. They didn't get it at first, but when I mentioned 'Combat,' they finally followed.
I was crouched at the peephole, watching the paper ring, guiding Avery Nolan with hand signals—just like a play in the field—then *snap*—the stick broke clean in half.
I gave the signal—just a nod, but it meant everything. Time to move.

I’m crouched low, peering through the periscope, watching that vacuum pipe creep toward the paper ring—just twelve inches away. My voice comes out tight through the coffee can, telling Roger it’s a go: 'A-okay... initiate retrieval suction.'
I felt the hose finally grip down there—suction had to be just right—and I shouted, 'We have suction! Pull it up! PULL IT UP!'
I hesitated at the doorway—just a second too long—and the vacuums were already whining, building up that crazy pressure behind me.
I stood there covered in dust, took my glasses off, and finally saw it—we’d been doing this all wrong. We needed total surprise, so I said it plain: we tunnel.
